title: Witness – a voice-anchored evidence recorder for AI coding agents
story_key: story|title:witness a voice anchored evidence recorder for ai coding agents
content_excerpt: Voice-anchored causal evidence recorder for AI coding agents — talk, point, and get an evidence package your agent can act on. 语音锚定的因果证据记录仪。 You experience the product and talk — “this button does nothing.” Witness welds every word to the causal evidence of that exact second: clicks, requests, console errors, DOM mutations, screenshots, full rrweb replay — then hands a structured evidence package to your AI coding agent. AI agents can't see what you see. Describing a visual bug costs ten minutes of screenshots and prompt crafting — and still loses the why . Voice is the cheapest annotation channel there is; it just never had a recorder. No downloads, no API keys. System Edge/Chrome is preferred; bundled Chromium is the fallback. events.jsonl streams to disk as you go — kill the process and you lose only the last few hundred milliseconds. wit recover rebuilds everything. Each spoken fragment lands on a timeline as a SAY block carrying the causal burst of that moment — dead clicks, mutations, errors — with linked shots and DOM snapshots. Agent-facing artifacts (PROMPT.md / SEGMENTS.md / session.md) are always generated in English — the most reliable corpus for LLMs; your words stay verbatim, never translated. wit mcp serves the session over stdio. Point any MCP-capable agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Devin) at it and it pulls exactly what it needs: list_segments · segment_detail(n) · session_overview · list_says · session_md · events_around(t_ms, radius, kinds) · get_errors · get_shot · get_body · get_dom_state(t) · get_asr · set_asr Voice-anchored causal evidence recorder for AI coding agents — talk, point, and get an evidence package your agent can act on. 语音锚定的因果证据记录仪。

title: Show HN: Give your agent its own temp mail service
story_key: story|title:give your agent its own temp mail service
content_excerpt: CLI and agent skill for a self-hosted cloudflare_temp_email instance: tiered addresses, codes and links, a local registry, and deploys. buzon is a CLI for a self-hosted cloudflare_temp_email instance, a mail server that runs on a Cloudflare Worker with D1. It creates addresses on your domain, waits for the verification code or magic link, and keeps a local record of which address belongs to which account. Public temp-mail services are blocked by most sign-up forms, and their inboxes are readable by anyone who guesses the name. A catch-all on your own domain avoids both, but turns into a pile of addresses nobody remembers. buzon puts a lifetime on each address, cleans up the short ones, and records the long ones. Or as a standalone binary, with no Bun needed, for linux-x64 , linux-arm64 , darwin-x64 or darwin-arm64 from the latest release : buzon reads its passwords from BUZON_SITE_PASSWORD and BUZON_ADMIN_PASSWORD , or else from the keyring: the Secret Service through secret-tool on Linux, the Keychain on macOS. No instance yet? docs/deploying.md goes from a domain on Cloudflare to a running one, mostly through buzon init --deploy . Point buzon at the instance. It checks that the instance answers, serves the domain and accepts the password before writing anything: skills/buzon teaches an agent to pick the tier, get a code or link, and find an address again later. Install it with: A test fails the build when the skill names a command or flag the CLI does not have. Cloudflare Email Routing hands every message for your domain to the Worker, which stores it in D1. A daily cron deletes expired ste and mte addresses by the tier in their name. buzon talks to the Worker over its HTTPS API, and keeps the registry of sites and notes on your machine only. CLI and agent skill for a self-hosted cloudflare_temp_email instance: tiered addresses, codes and links, a local registry, and deploys.

title: LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
summary: We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
summary: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. We compare three decision models and three general LLMs as actors and judges on ALFWorld, and use JEV as a teacher on ALFWorld and WebShop. As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

title: Show HN: I built a tool to check website access for 14 AI crawlers
story_key: story|title:i built a tool to check website access for 14 ai crawlers
content_excerpt: Enter a URL. The checker reads its robots.txt, requests the page with the user agent of 14 AI crawlers, and compares each answer with a normal browser request. You get a verdict per crawler and the line to change. robots.txt says what a crawler may fetch. Your CDN decides what it actually gets. Public http(s) pages only. One check sends about 18 requests to that site, 14 of them headers-only, and usually takes a few seconds. Partial it can fetch the page, but something limits use: noindex, nosnippet, rate limiting, almost no text without JavaScript, or a robots.txt rule a user-initiated agent may not follow. Blocked robots.txt disallows the URL, robots.txt is unreachable, or the server refuses that user agent while serving a browser. Unknown our request can't settle it, for example when the site refuses every request from our server or verifies crawler IP addresses. Tokens, purposes and user agents checked against each vendor's documentation on November 6, 2026 . robots.txt is a request to the crawler; your CDN, firewall or hosting can still refuse the request. Cloudflare's AI crawler controls, managed bot rules and some hosting “bad bot” filters block by user agent. The report shows the status code each user agent received next to the browser's. That is a business choice. Vendors now split the jobs: GPTBot versus OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot versus Claude-SearchBot, Google-Extended versus Googlebot. Google states that Google-Extended does not affect inclusion in Google Search, and OpenAI lists GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot as separate settings. Check each vendor's page linked above before you split rules. No major vendor in this list documents llms.txt as a crawling or ranking input. The checker reports it because some tools and agents read it; see do you need llms.txt . No. The check runs on request and the report goes back to your browser only; the checker keeps no database of URLs or results. Hosting access logs may record the request like any page view.

title: codex 0.169.0
summary:
New Features

  • The opt-in terminal workspace supports multiple side-chat tabs. Switch between them with the keyboard or mouse, and reopen saved local side chats after restarting Codex. (#59784, #60152, #60181)
  • Search older tasks from the agent command center by name, prompt preview, or working directory. (#60286)
  • Turn on Collapse turn details in the full-screen transcript to fold completed activity beneath each prompt while keeping answers visible and tool output searchable. (#60554, #60555, #60556, #60557)
  • Add or edit custom model providers from the terminal. With custom gateway onboarding enabled, you can create a provider during sign-in and use a device code for supported gateways over SSH or without a local browser. (#59779, #60009, #60186, #60486, #60662)
  • Press Ctrl+S in the terminal report editor to save a diagnostic ZIP locally, even when uploads are disabled. (#60542)
  • With the opt-in Cloud connection on macOS and Linux, send images, choose a model and reasoning effort, and archive or restore Cloud conversations from the terminal. (#59828, #60061, #60635, #60651)

Bug Fixes

  • codex exec keeps project configuration and MCP servers disabled in untrusted directories, even with --sandbox workspace-write. Use --trust with codex exec or codex review to explicitly save project trust. (#60041)
  • Yes, clear context and implement now hands the full approved plan to the fresh session and keeps the current session open if the handoff fails. (#60763)
  • Fixed Windows sandbox handling for quoted cmd.exe paths and for PowerShell sessions whose working directory has an unreadable parent. (#60624, #60647)
  • Pasted images on macOS retain their intended orientation and use native PNG or JPEG clipboard data when available. (#60455)
  • The terminal no longer stays busy waiting for MCP servers that a shared app server did not report. (#60280, #60622)
  • Interrupted turns now close cleanly, and delayed aborts or file approval cancellations no longer interrupt a later turn. (#59910, #60700)

Documentation

  • Updated the openai-docs skill to focus on Codex and ChatGPT Work questions and first-time API setup, with dedicated guidance for configuring Codex across a team. (#59944, #59949)
  • Documented how app-server clients can list models or authorize a gateway for a configured provider without changing the default provider. (#59776, #59819)

Chores

  • Updated bundled SQLite to 3.54 to pick up write-ahead log fixes. (#60432)
  • Plugin marketplace upgrades can reuse Git objects already on disk, reducing repeat downloads. (#60528)

title: Sandbox resourcing: burst, don't reserve
summary: Why you're paying for capacity you aren't using, and how to pay only for what you use.
story_key: story|title:sandbox resourcing burst don t reserve
content_excerpt: Across Modal, a typical Sandbox spends more than half its life using less than 6% of its peak CPU. Take a coding agent: the Sandbox sits nearly idle while the model reasons about what to do next, and spikes only when the agent installs dependencies, runs tests, or builds the project. The same pattern shows up in other common Sandbox workloads: RL rollouts, evals, and app builders. Today, most sandboxes are priced based on a fixed-resource reservation model. Reservations are a poor fit for spiky work, for two reasons: We believe your bill should align with your workload, rising when it’s busy and falling when it’s idle. That’s why our Sandboxes burst: a Sandbox gets the CPU and memory it needs when your work spikes and gives them back when it is done. You pay for what you actually use. Every Sandbox bursts by default. Start with the base 0.125 cores and 128 MiB request and let your Sandbox grow as it needs. With active-resource pricing, you pay each second for what you use, with the small request as a floor. You can request more to guarantee it, but you’ll pay for those resources even when your Sandbox is idle. You can also set a limit to cap how far your Sandbox can burst; think of it as setting the size of the computer the Sandbox lives on. Most workloads don’t need to set a request or limit: use the default and burst from there. Because you pay for what you use, estimate your costs from average usage rather than peak usage: CPU cost ≈ runtime × CPU rate × average cores used Memory cost ≈ runtime × memory rate × average GiB used This average works for bursting Sandboxes because each second, a Sandbox is billed for the higher of its request and what it actually uses. Since the average sits well below the peak, customers with bursty workloads can end up paying a fraction of their typical reservation bill. Your Sandbox is guaranteed its request, which is small by default. When it bursts beyond that, it draws from a shared pool of the machine’s idle capacity, which Modal’s scheduler keeps free on every machine. It works because of the law of averages. Sandboxes sharing a machine mostly run unrelated work for different customers, so they rarely spike at the same moment. If every Sandbox reserved capacity for its peak, the machine would need room for the sum of all the peaks. With bursting, it only needs room for the most they use at the same time. It’s the same reason a power grid can be much smaller than the sum of every household’s peak demand. For most work

content_excerpt: Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
summary: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

title: Lost in Delegation: Studying the Effectiveness of Task Orchestration in Generative Search
summary: LLMs have quickly evolved from models used in isolation to agentic systems that delegate tasks to external tools and other LLMs to solve complex assignments. This agentic augmentation has led to impressive capability gains. However, when and how delegation improves performance remains poorly understood. For example, it is unclear whether delegation helps when tasks involve post-cutoff information that the orchestrating LLM cannot reliably resolve from its own knowledge. In this work, we use purpose-built datasets with pre- and post-cutoff splits to compare various delegation modes. We find that delegation provides no consistent accuracy improvement over non-delegated setups, with effects varying across models and tasks. When tasks involve knowledge unavailable to the orchestrator, delegation can substantially degrade accuracy, while direct tool use with the same LLM performs much better. Our analysis identifies distorted delegated queries, inefficient tool use, and failures to preserve and use information between agents as recurring failure modes. These findings suggest that effective orchestration requires both well-calibrated delegation decisions and effective exchange of information between agents.

title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
summary: Eval-driven development helps you build AI agents against a consistent set of metrics. Define good behavior, write the eval first, then compare experiments.
story_key: story|title:what is eval driven development how to improve ai agents
content_excerpt: Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse. Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench ), and have boiled it down to a three step process: In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process. The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic: As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it ( LLM-as-a-judge ). With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them. The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent. EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers: Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. Our spec looks like this: We’ll evaluate on these guidelines, even though the agent doesn’t have the capability yet. Build a d

  • Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
  • Fixed claude -p on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
  • Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
  • Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty claude mcp list output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
  • Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
  • Improved the /model picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
  • Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the /device page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
  • Improved claude install and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
  • Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
  • Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
  • Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
  • Improved the agent view's row for a claude --bg --worktree session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
  • Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: /login is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
  • Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
  • Improved claude remote-control's messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
  • Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
  • Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
  • Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
  • Updated the session-feedback message and the allowedProviders setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the forceLoginMethod description to cover every paid Claude plan
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
  • Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
  • Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed allowUnsandboxedCommands: false or allowManagedDomainsOnly, and not to load in dontAsk mode
  • Changed mods' own tool calls ($.tool.call, $.mcp.call) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in dontAsk and -p runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
  • Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to fable: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use /model claude-fable-5-1 to switch back
  • Changed the fast mode labels in /fast, /config and /model to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders inside ~/.claude/plugins no longer load when Claude works on files there
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
  • Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
  • Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of num_hooks and num_success after Bash and PowerShell calls
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
  • Changed AskUserQuestion in claude -p and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented afkTimeoutMs input field
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
  • Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
  • Changed policy_mode: layered in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, match: {} included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
  • Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL variables in the gateway's environment. Set base_url on the upstream to use another endpoint
  • Changed headless sessions to reload mods in .claude/skills when their files change; set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0 to turn this off
  • Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
  • Changed cp and mv spelled by a path, such as /bin/cp, to get the same path checks as cp and mv
  • Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
  • Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
  • Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and names a User-Agent, without asking, so other commands and scheduled runs no longer stop at its prompt
  • Changed Remote Control sessions to keep the folder they were started in: a connected client can no longer move a session to another folder
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces take-overs from an undeclared source: saved data is set aside for cleanupPeriodDays, and options and secrets until claude plugin restore-set-aside
  • [VSCode] Added a warning above the prompt box when both an auth token and an API key are set, matching the terminal's startup warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed a plugin's permission request showing a name with hidden characters: it now reads "a plugin"
